segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Simeon Peter, a slave and apostle of Jesus Christ, to those who have received a faith of equal standing with ours through the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ:

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: May grace and peace be multiplied to you in the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: His divine power has given us everything needed for life and godliness, through the knowledge of the one who called us by his own glory and excellence.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Through these he has given us the precious and very great promises, so that through them you may become sharers in the divine nature, having escaped the decay that is in the world because of desire.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this very reason, make every effort to supply in your faith excellence, and in excellence knowledge,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and in knowledge self-control, and in self-control endurance, and in endurance godliness,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and in godliness brotherly affection, and in brotherly affection love.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For when these things are yours and are increasing, they keep you from being idle or unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For whoever lacks these things is nearsighted to the point of blindness, having forgotten the cleansing of their former sins.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Therefore, brothers and sisters, put all the more effort into making your calling and election sure; for if you do these things you will never stumble.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For in this way the entrance into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ will be richly supplied to you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Therefore I intend always to remind you of these things, even though you know them and are firmly established in the truth that you have.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I consider it right, as long as I am in this tent, to rouse you with a reminder,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: since I know that the putting off of my tent is coming soon, as indeed our Lord Jesus Christ made clear to me.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I will make every effort so that after my departure you will be able at any time to call these things to mind.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we were not following cleverly devised myths when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ; on the contrary, we had been eyewitnesses of his majesty.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For he received honor and glory from God the Father when a voice such as this was borne to him by the Majestic Glory:

segments.speaker: God
segments.text: “This is my Son, my beloved, in whom I delight.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: We ourselves heard this voice borne from heaven when we were with him on the holy mountain.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So we have the prophetic word made all the more sure, and you do well to pay attention to it as to a lamp shining in a murky place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Know this first of all: no prophecy of Scripture comes about by anyone’s own interpretation,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for no prophecy was ever borne by human will; rather, human beings, borne along by the Holy Spirit, spoke from God.

notes.note: The Greek has the Semitic spelling Symeōn rather than the usual ‘Simon’; it is used of Peter elsewhere only in Acts 15:14. Some manuscripts read the more familiar ‘Simon’, and many English versions print that form.

Most English versions have ‘servant’. The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, a person owned by a master, and a first-century reader would have heard it that way. In the Septuagint ‘slave of the Lord’ is also a title of honor for figures such as Moses, David and the prophets. Some recent translations likewise use ‘slave’.

notes.phrase: our God and Savior Jesus Christ
notes.traditional: of God and our Saviour Jesus Christ
notes.note: The Greek has a single article governing both nouns, the same construction as ‘our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ’ in verse 11. Most grammarians and modern translations therefore take it as calling Jesus both God and Savior. The alternative, ‘of our God and of the Savior Jesus Christ’, which distinguishes two persons as verse 2 does, is possible and is found in some older versions.

The Greek word is the standard term in Greek ethics for virtue or moral excellence, and was also used of a god’s displayed power and renown. The same word returns in verse 5 for a quality believers are to supply, and ‘excellence’ is used in both places so that the echo can be heard. Translations vary between ‘virtue’, ‘goodness’ and ‘excellence’, often using different words in the two verses.

Traditionally ‘corruption’. The Greek word means perishing, decay or ruin, the opposite of the imperishability that belongs to the divine nature; in modern English ‘corruption’ chiefly suggests bribery or dishonesty. Moral ruin is included, since the decay is said to come through desire, and most translations keep ‘corruption’.

notes.traditional: I think it meet; I think it right
notes.note: This word-family is normally rendered ‘righteous’ or ‘just’ in this translation. Here the adjective is used impersonally in a common idiom meaning that something is proper or fitting, so ‘right’ is used. Greek has one word-family where English divides between right/righteous and just/justice; ‘righteousness’ in verse 1 belongs to the same family.

Peter speaks of his body as a tent, a temporary shelter soon to be taken down; older versions have ‘tabernacle’ and some modern ones simply ‘body’. Paul uses similar imagery in 2 Corinthians 5:1–4. The word for ‘departure’ in verse 15 is exodos, the same word Luke uses for Jesus’s death in his account of the transfiguration (Luke 9:31).

The Greek adjective can mean ‘soon’ or ‘swift, sudden’, so the sense may be that Peter’s death is near or that it will come suddenly; most translations choose ‘soon’. What Jesus ‘made clear’ is usually connected with the saying about Peter’s death in John 21:18–19, though the letter does not say so.

The Greek word was used for the arrival and presence of a ruler or dignitary on an official visit, and among early Christians for the future arrival of Jesus in glory. Most interpreters take it that way here, with the transfiguration described in the next verses offered as a preview that guarantees it. A minority think the reference is to his first coming.

notes.traditional: came (of the voice and of prophecy); moved or carried along (of the prophets)
notes.note: The same Greek verb, ‘carry’ or ‘bear’, is used four times in this passage: of the voice in verses 17 and 18, and in verse 21 of prophecy and of the prophets. Most translations vary the English, which hides the link drawn between the voice from heaven and the prophetic word. ‘Borne’ is used each time here to keep it.

notes.traditional: a more sure word of prophecy
notes.note: The Greek says literally ‘we have the prophetic word more sure’. This can mean that the prophetic word has been confirmed by what the apostles saw on the mountain, as rendered here and in many modern translations. It can also mean that the prophetic word is something even more sure than that experience, as in the older tradition. Some take the comparative simply as ‘altogether reliable’.

The Greek is terse: literally, no prophecy of Scripture ‘comes to be of one’s own interpretation’. The rendering here takes this of the prophecy’s origin: it did not arise from the prophet’s own reading of events, which fits the explanation in verse 21. The other long-standing reading applies it to the reader: no prophecy is a matter for private interpretation. Scholars are divided.

candidates.reason: Recurs throughout the New Testament as a literal status and as a self-description of apostles and believers, and translations split between ‘servant’, ‘bondservant’ and ‘slave’.

The plural address to mixed congregations occurs in nearly every letter, and the choice between ‘brothers’, ‘brothers and sisters’ and ‘friends’ should be made once, together with compounds such as φιλαδελφία.
The standard Hellenistic word for piety recurs in the Pastoral Letters, Acts and 2 Peter, and ‘godliness’, ‘piety’, ‘devotion’ and ‘reverence’ are all defensible but should not alternate.
Recurs in Romans 8, 1 Corinthians 15, Galatians 6 and 2 Peter 2 with the φθαρτός/ἄφθαρτος family, where the traditional ‘corruption’ now suggests dishonesty where the Greek means perishing or decay.
With ἐκλεκτός and ἐκλέγομαι it recurs across Paul, Peter and the Gospels, and ‘election/elect’ versus ‘choice/chosen’ needs one decision, since ‘election’ now suggests voting.
